Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions chosen from any ONE SECTION ONLY. All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

questions.enonce_markdown: a) What is a Surah in Islam? (5 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown: A surah is a chapter of the Qur'an. The Qur'an has 114 surahs of very different lengths, from the long Surah 2 (Al-Baqara) to short ones of only a few verses. Each surah is made of verses (ayat) and has a name, such as Al-Fatiha ("The Opening") or Al-Baqara ("The Cow"). The surahs are arranged in the Qur'an in an order that is not the order of their revelation: the longer ones come first, with the exception of the opening surah. Muslims believe that the arrangement was settled under the guidance of the Prophet. Surahs are traditionally classed as Makkan (revealed before the Hijra) or Madinan (revealed after it). Nearly every surah begins with the formula "In the name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful" (the Bismillah); Surah 9 (At-Tawba) is the usual exception.
themes: A Level Religious Studies - the quran in islam

questions.enonce_markdown: b) In what ways does Surah 2 (Al-Bagara) reflect a typical Medina surah? (20 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The Qur'an in the form we have it is a collection of Makkan and Madinan surahs. Madinan surahs were revealed after the Hijra (622 CE), when the Muslims formed a community and a state in Madinah. Surah 2 is the longest surah, with 286 verses, and Muslims hold that it was revealed mostly in the early years in Madinah. It shows many features of a typical Madinan surah. (The question prints the name as "Al-Bagara"; the usual spelling is Al-Baqara.)

**1. Length and style.** Madinan surahs are generally long, with long verses written in a detailed, legislative style, in contrast to the short, rhythmic, powerful verses of many Makkan surahs. Surah 2 is the longest of the Qur'an and contains the longest verse (the verse of debt, 2:282).

**2. Legal and social rulings.** Madinan surahs lay down rules for a community. Surah 2 contains rules on fasting in Ramadan (2:183 to 185), pilgrimage, the change of the direction of prayer (qibla) from Jerusalem towards the Ka'ba, marriage, divorce and waiting periods, treatment of orphans, charity, usury (riba), debts and contracts, and fighting in defence of the community, in addition to bequests and retaliation.

**3. Address to the community.** The phrase "O you who believe" is typical of the Madinan surahs, and it appears often in Surah 2. Makkan surahs more often address "O people" or "O mankind".

**4. Dealing with the People of the Book.** In Madinah the Muslims lived beside Jewish tribes and Christians. Surah 2 recalls at length the history of the Children of Israel (Musa, the golden calf, the story of the cow from which the surah takes its name) and discusses Ibrahim and the Ka'ba, and it speaks of the covenant and of disagreements with earlier communities.

**5. The hypocrites (munafiqun).** The opening part of the surah (verses 8 to 20) describes the hypocrites, people who professed belief without sincerity. This group appeared in Madinah, not in Makkah, where opposition was open.

**6. Organisation of the community.** The surah deals with spending in the way of God, mutual support, justice, and the duty of being "a community of the middle way" (the ummah), reflecting a time when the Muslims had to organise themselves.

**7. Theology and worship also present.** Like other Madinan surahs, Surah 2 also affirms basic beliefs: the oneness of God, the prophets, the scriptures, the angels and the Last Day (as in 2:177 and 2:285 to 286), and contains the Throne verse (Ayat al-Kursi, 2:255), showing the continuity of the Makkan themes.

**Conclusion.** Surah 2 reflects the typical features of a Madinan surah: its length, its legal and social rulings, its address to "those who believe", its dealing with the People of the Book and the hypocrites, and its concern for a community. It also keeps the basic doctrines of faith revealed in Makkah.
